items.desc: Design Miami 2026 Preview: “Unveiling” Works From 75 International Galleries at This Year’s Miami Art Week Design Miami, one of the most exciting events of Miami Art Week, is back for the 22nd edition of its flagship fair. The event, devoted to contemporary collectible design, returns to the Miami Beach Convention Center with a lineup of 75 international galleries, museum-quality presentations, an
items.text:
Brodin, “Constellation of Memory,” 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Kelley and Gavin Brodin.)
Design Miami , one of the most exciting events of Miami Art Week, is back for the 22nd edition of its flagship fair. The event, devoted to contemporary collectible design, returns to the Miami Beach Convention Center with a lineup of 75 international galleries, museum-quality presentations, and a curatorial theme that celebrates the creatives behind the works on display.
The theme, Unveiling , calls for the viewers to truly observe each object, deciphering what inspired the artist to create them, and the surrounding stories behind their choices. These may be hiding in plain sight or several times removed from the final result, reflecting something deeply personal or rooted in the artist’s culture. Unveiling is then divided among four curatorial threads, each with different approaches and best represented by certain artists, techniques, and galleries.
Pippin Drysdale, “Sacred Lands,” 2026. Adrian Sassoon at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Adrian Sassoon, London; photography by Robert Frith, Acorn Photo.)
First up is Process as Aesthetic: Unveiling the Hand of the Maker . This theme highlights the creative process, particularly the techniques, labor, and experimentation that come to determine an object’s aesthetic, regarding these steps as a vehicle for expression. This can be seen in the ceramic works of Bouke de Vries and Pippin Drysdale; Caroline Desile’s architecture-influenced Totem 1 ; Richard Haining’s STACKED creations, made up of thousands of pieces of salvaged New York City wood; and Man Ray’s Optic-Topic mask , the centerpiece of this division.
Le Corbusier, “La licorne passe sur la mer,” 1959. Boccara Gallery at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Boccara Gallery.)
Meanwhile, Subverting Archetypes: The Familiar, Reimagined , takes a more surrealist route, blurring the line between the familiar and the uncanny, asking viewers to reassess to what they think they know. Such is the case of a selection of 20th-century tapestries by Le Corbusier, Sonia Delaunay, and Alexander Calder. This section also features the work of Brazilian designer Lucas Recchia, who blends metal with fused glass, and a wall piece by Jaydan Moore, who turns found, silver-plated tableware into sculptural forms.
Dee Clements, “Gams,” 2026. Mindy Solomon Gallery at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: Clare Britt, courtesy of the artist and Mindy Solomon Gallery)

items.title: 89 People Who Missed The Joke So Completely It Became Funnier Than The Joke Itself
items.desc: Some people can spot a joke from a mile away, while others need the punchline explained. From painfully missed sarcasm to jokes taken far too seriously, these funny interactions show what happens when humor goes completely over someone's head. Pandas, get ready to have a good laugh!
items.text:
Understanding a joke actually involves a bit of brainwork. Researchers used brain scans to study how people process humor and found that the brain has to recognize something unexpected in a joke and work out its intended meaning.
This process involves several areas associated with language and understanding meaning, which help us connect the punchline to the rest of what was said. So, even a short joke can require a little mental gymnastics.
Sarcasm can be very tricky because people don't always mean what their words literally say. Someone might say, "Well, that went wonderfully," after dropping their phone into a puddle. The sentence sounds positive, but the situation tells a completely different story.
To understand the real meaning, listeners have to connect what was said with what's happening around them. A study examined how people recognize spoken sarcasm and found that both surrounding context and the speaker's tone help listeners determine whether a comment is sincere or sarcastic. Without those clues, a sarcastic remark can sound like a very strange compliment.
Social cues make a big difference in understanding and processing jokes. A raised eyebrow, a playful smile, or an exaggerated voice can signal that a comment isn't meant to be taken literally. A study found that people rely on different kinds of information when interpreting nonliteral language, including social conventions and changes in tone.
These cues help listeners recognize when someone is being ironic or communicating something beyond the literal meaning of their words. This also explains why a joke delivered with a completely straight face can be harder to understand. Sometimes, the speaker thinks their playful intention is obvious, while the listener is left trying to work out what they actually mean.
A joke might fall flat because the listener doesn't have the background information needed to understand it. Some jokes rely on knowing a particular movie, following a celebrity scandal, or remembering something that happened earlier in a conversation.
A 2024 paper explains that understanding a joke often depends on connecting its punchline to background knowledge and contextual clues. If everyone else knows the reference except you, their laughter can feel like an invitation to a party you weren't told about.

items.title: 69 Dystopian Images That Look Like Scenes From Unrealistic Movies But They Are Our Current Reality
items.desc: The USA has recently been stuck in a dystopian state, and American netizens are opening up about it online. We have compiled some of the most disturbing posts that reveal the nightmarish life people face every day. You might recognize some of these issues, while others may surprise you. Scroll through the whole list at your own discretion!
items.text:
While many problems drag people down, let’s focus on the persistent ones. As you scroll through the list, you will realize that Americans are really sick and tired of AI. It’s being forced down people’s throats like there’s no tomorrow, and not everyone is happy about it.
In fact, according to a recent poll , a 57% majority of Americans say AI is bad for society, while 42% say it is good for society. Only 2% say it is “extremely” good for society, while 17% say it is extremely bad.
When folks were asked about the risks of AI, they stated the following reasons: hacking secure computer systems, eliminating many jobs, people losing their ability to make their own decisions without AI, increasing economic inequality, and human extinction.
However, a minority of poll respondents said AI is living up to its promises: making everyday tasks easier, strengthening U.S. dominance in AI technology, boosting productivity, and creating many new jobs.
Meanwhile, most people say the federal government is not doing enough to regulate AI. Also, two-thirds of Americans (66%) oppose building new data centers in the U.S., and that number rises to 72% when asked about building one in their community.
While many people oppose AI, tech leaders have also warned that out-of-control AI poses profound risks to society and humanity. These dangers far outweigh the benefits.
And while we are on the subject of artificial intelligence, many Americans blamed it for the recent outages that they faced. From banks to email, everything seemed to be falling apart. However, there’s no evidence to blame AI, and the fields that faced these outages have been talking about bugs they detected.
Another major concern Americans expressed was the rise of subscription culture and how they’re done being ambushed by ads everywhere. Every year, CNET dives into the state of subscriptions to find out how much US adults spend on subscriptions and on which types of services.
This year, they found that US adults’ top subscription is streaming, and they’re spending an average of $111 a month on subscriptions, totaling $1,332 annually. Even more unsettling, US adults waste an average of $21 a month (or $252 annually) on unused subscriptions. These include streaming apps, gym memberships, music subscriptions, and more. Shockingly, it’s up from $204 last year.

Created around 1520 by German artist Albrecht Altdorfer, A Thickly Wooded Landscape With a Rainbow Behind the Trees and a
items.text:
A post shared by Italian Old Masters (chiefly!) (@oldmasters_jlvieites)
A rare Renaissance painting that has remained out of public view for nearly 70 years is heading to auction. Created around 1520 by German artist Albrecht Altdorfer, A Thickly Wooded Landscape With a Rainbow Behind the Trees and a Distant Outcrop to the Right Beneath a Cloud-Laden Sky will lead Sotheby’s Old Master and 19th Century Paintings Evening Auction in London on December 9, 2026. The auction house estimates the small but historically significant work to sell for £3 million to £5 million (approximately $3.9 million to $6.5 million).
The painting recently resurfaced in a private Swiss collection. Its discovery has drawn attention from art historians because it represents only the third known independent landscape in oil by Altdorfer. The other two belong to the National Gallery in London and the Alte Pinakothek in Munich. No known painting by the artist has appeared at auction since 1980, making the upcoming sale an especially rare opportunity for collectors and museums.
Unlike many Renaissance paintings that use landscapes as backdrops for religious or historical scenes, Altdorfer places nature at the center of the composition. The small painting measures just 23.4 by 19.8 centimeters (approximately 9 by 8 inches), yet its intricate details create an immersive woodland scene filled with dense trees, tangled undergrowth, and a distant castle perched on a rocky outcrop.
A rainbow arcs above the treetops, catching the light beneath a sky heavy with clouds. The subtle shift in atmosphere gives the scene a sense of depth and quiet drama. Altdorfer’s distinctive treatment of foliage also reflects his interest in the forests surrounding Regensburg, the German city where he spent much of his life.
The artwork once belonged to the aristocratic House of Harrach in Vienna. In 1957, the current owner’s father acquired it from the family’s collection. It has remained with the family ever since, largely escaping public attention and scholarly research until its identification in 2026.
The discovery expands the known body of work by an artist widely regarded as a pioneer of independent landscape painting in Western art. Altdorfer helped establish a new approach to the genre in which forests, mountains, and atmospheric conditions became subjects in their own right.

items.desc: While a little boy was fighting a deadly disease in the Children’s Hospital of New Orleans he longed for a place to go get some fresh air or distraction from his woes. Before he died, he and his family started a foundation to raise money—and five years later his wish was fulfilled. Last week, his […] The post World’s First Museum Built in a Children’s Hospital Fulfills Dying Boy’s Wish For Playtim
items.text:
While a little boy was fighting a deadly disease in the Children’s Hospital of New Orleans he longed for a place to go get some fresh air or distraction from his woes. Before he died, he and his family started a foundation to raise money—and five years later his wish was fulfilled.
Last week, his family celebrated the opening of the world’s first museum incorporated into a hospital—a fantastical ‘Imaginarium’ where sick kids and their families can go for art, movement, pretending, and fun.
Named after the nine-year-old, Walker Beery, Walker’s Imaginarium is a 15,000-square-foot children’s museum where patients can wander through rooms interacting with uniquely Louisiana themes: dancing to cajun music, exploring a bayou, joining a Mardi Gras parade, or enjoying a quiet moment among an animated fish tank.
Designed for a range of physical, sensory, and medical needs, kids in wheelchairs can play both mini-golf and foosball while rolling by the colorful ramps and murals—and forgetting they’re in a hospital. (See the video at the bottom…)
For the Beery family, Walker’s Imaginarium is a deeply personal expression of their son Walker’s vision to give back to others. In August 2019, he was diagnosed with pediatric brain cancer, yet through surgeries, hospital stays, and chemotherapy treatments, Walker’s infectious courage and grateful spirit always amazed his family and all who encountered him during his two-year battle at the hospital, recently renamed Manning Family Children’s.
Walker’s Imaginarium was funded entirely through philanthropic support and donations raised by the community and the lad’s foundation, Kids Join The Fight .
“Walker’s spirit is carried forward in the joy that is embedded in this amazing project,” said Walker’s dad Taylor, co-founder of Kids Join The Fight.
“Every child who finds a moment of escape, every family that experiences joy together carries Walker’s dream forward: to use his own experience to make someone else’s a little easier, and a little happier.”
Designed around the needs of young patients, the interactive experiences use therapeutic play to relieve the burden of long hospitalizations and support holistic recovery.
By integrating feedback from clinical experts and patient families, the design team transformed health challenges into opportunities for play-based healing.
From the very first step into Walker’s Imaginarium, visitors are invited to create their own dance party, complete with interactive lights, marching band music

items.title: Good News in History, November 21
items.desc: This daily column features all the good news, anniversaries and birthdays from this day in history—November 21. The post Good News in History, November 21 appeared first on Good News Network .
items.text:
52 years ago today, Congress voted in a two-thirds majority to override President Gerald Ford’s attempted veto of the Freedom of Information Act , after he was influenced to try the veto by Dick Cheney and Donald Rumsfeld. That decision gave the country the FOIA which it still maintains today, out of which have come dozens of the most high-profile news stories and political scandals in modern American history. READ some of the stories this law has made possible to report… (1974)
Any US citizen or private entity can make an application under FOIA. Agencies and departments under only the executive branch then must turn over all the requested information in a timely manner. If the petitioner has cause to believe the agency is delaying, impeding, or even tampering with the material, they can seek recourse to a Special Council.
FOIA requests can be fairly expensive, and today, only a limited number of publications and individuals can afford to petition for all the records they might need for a story.
FOIA requests have revealed shocking stories. Most prominently in the last few years, a huge FOIA push by the Washington Post gathered tens of thousands of documents from the Office of the Inspector General for the War in Afghanistan, revealing a depth of corruption, political and military nihilism, incompetence, and wastefulness that few Americans knew about.
Other famous cases involve the receiving of documents that show America almost blew up a hydrogen bomb over North Carolina in 1961, and that the FBI had been secretly surveilling African-American writers for decades starting in 1919.
Also recently discovered were years of email correspondences between Dr. Anthony Fauci, the NIH, and the Wuhan Institute of Virology which showed the NIH was funding gain of function research on coronaviruses there.
243 years ago today, the world’s first untethered hot-air balloon flight took off at around 2 p.m. from the garden of the Château de la Muette in the Bois de Boulogne. In the presence of the King of France, Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier and Marquis François Laurent d’Arlandes, enjoyed a 25-minute flight that traveled slowly about 5½ miles (some 9 km) to the southeast, attaining an altitude of 3,000 feet, before returning to the ground at the Butte-aux-Cailles on the outskirts of Paris.

items.text:
Shengwei Dai, “Bishwa Ijtema2.” Absolute Winner of the Black and White Photo Awards 2026.
The Black and White Photo Awards were created in 2022 to uplift photographers who have made B&W photography their medium of choice. Now in its fifth year, this international photography contest returns with new categories and bigger prizes than ever.
This year, the Absolute Winner of the Black and White Photo Awards was Shengwei Dai from China. His image, titled Bishwa Ijtema2 , captures a man leaping between two trains as people watch from the roofs, doors, and windows of the train cars.
“The image stands out for its perspective, placing the viewer between the two trains and transforming the space separating them into the setting for an extraordinary composition,” says the Black and White Photo Awards team. “The lines of the train cars draw the eye toward the figure suspended in the air, while the faces of those witnessing the leap complete a scene filled with energy, tension, and detail.”
Dai received a cash award of €1,500 ($1,647), the largest monetary prize awarded in the competition’s five-year history. And this year; in addition to the existing Architecture, Street, Portrait, Fauna and Flora, and Landscape categories; the competition also introduced Open Theme. This new category offers a space for artistic, narrative, and conceptual compositions that don’t fit into any of the aforementioned groupings. The inaugural Open Theme Category Winner was Lloyd Lane with Convergence , a photograph that shows a flock of starlings flying over Brighton Palace Pier in England. Lane and the other five category winners each received a €200 ($220) prize.
Now that the winners have been announced, the Black and White Photo Awards team is looking forward to the next edition of the contest. For those hoping to take part, the organizers announced that entries for the Black and White Photo Awards 2027 will open on January 1, 2027. To learn more about the contest and submit your entries, visit the Black and White Photo Awards website .

items.desc: JoyDrops champions awards-eligible documentary shorts about joy, a counterweight to a category often dominated by tragedy. Good News Network has partnered with JoyDrops to spotlight these films and talk with the filmmakers behind them. “Believe me, it never gets old,” Freddie Nole told GNN. “I’m serious.” Nole is talking about the moment he meets a […] The post Freddie Nole Waits at the Prison Gat
items.text:
JoyDrops champions awards-eligible documentary shorts about joy, a counterweight to a category often dominated by tragedy. Good News Network has partnered with JoyDrops to spotlight these films and talk with the filmmakers behind them.
“Believe me, it never gets old,” Freddie Nole told GNN. “I’m serious.”
Nole is talking about the moment he meets a man walking out of prison, often someone with no one else coming to get him. He and his wife, Sue, take the man to a meal, buy him clothes, get him a phone and drive him to wherever he’s headed next. No two pickups are the same, he said, but one thing always is.
“The appreciation that these individuals express to us for just being there,” Nole said, “at a time when they’re most vulnerable.”
That work is at the heart of The Second Life of Freddie Nole , the latest film in GNN’s JoyDrops series.
Directed by Dana Nachman, the film rides along with Nole for a single day as he picks up a man leaving prison in Pennsylvania. Along the way, viewers learn that Nole knows this road personally. His full backstory comes only at the end.
Nachman, whose company, Sweet World Films, focuses on stories about repairing the world, had worked on wrongful conviction cases for years. But reentry was new to her. She and her business partner, Chelsea Matter, had a little money left over from another project and wanted a story that truly fit a short. A one-day road trip was the perfect container.
They reached out to Nole over Zoom. “Literally maybe 30 seconds of talking, I was like, oh God, this guy is special,” Nachman told GNN. “We call him movie gold. Freddie is life gold.”
She later learned that groups across the country do similar work, some just 50 miles from her home in Northern California. She’s glad she didn’t know sooner. “My ignorance got me to him, really,” she said.
Nole went to prison in 1969, when Richard Nixon was president. When he finally walked out, the only person he could count on was his wife, who had stood by him for more than 37 years.
He had sent her his clothing sizes so he wouldn’t stand out. They didn’t fit. “It was just a whole embarrassing situation for me,” he told GNN, “not so much the people, but that I was so detached from this normal society.”
Then he learned he was already in violation of his parole for not reporting in time. He spent four hours of his first night of freedom at the parole office. “My whole first day of being out was simply walking on pins and needles,” he said.

items.title: Breath of a Whale Captured by Drone Allows Full Genome Sequencing Without Intrusion
items.desc: The exhale from a whale’s blowhole has been captured by drones, and used to complete the genome sequencing of one of the ocean giants for the first time. Researchers from the University of St. Andrews in Scotland were part of an international team to sequence a whole genome using samples from whale breath collected by […] The post Breath of a Whale Captured by Drone Allows Full Genome Sequencing W
items.text:
The exhale from a whale’s blowhole has been captured by drones, and used to complete the genome sequencing of one of the ocean giants for the first time.
Researchers from the University of St. Andrews in Scotland were part of an international team to sequence a whole genome using samples from whale breath collected by a small aerial drone.
It marks the first time sequencing has been completed without the use of physical interventions—commonly using darts and biopsies collected by boat, which disturbs the animals, or from stranded mammals or historical specimens.
In some places and for some species this isn’t possible.
Yet, genomic data is “critical” for conservation, enabling researchers to measure population health, genetic diversity and inbreeding, as well as to identify individuals for “mark-recapture” studies, determine sex, and estimate population size.
To overcome the collection challenge, the team attached sterile petri dishes to a small drone. ( See below… )
They flew it through the exhaled breaths of one humpback whale at a time, which typically has one to six breaths per surfacing.
They collected 58 blow samples from 26 individual humpback whales in the Kitimat Fjord System in northern British Columbia, Canada.
Around 84% of the DNA in the blow came from the whale itself.
Repeat samples from the same whales, collected in different encounters and across two years, gave matching genomes—with the most upwind whale in a group targeted, to avoid mixing DNA from different animals.
More than a third of samples required no boat at all—only flying the drone directly from land.
Before the new study, only one North Pacific humpback’s whole genome had ever been publicly available.
After collection, DNA was sequenced to produce low-coverage nuclear genomes—inherited from both parents—and high-coverage mitochondrial genomes, inherited just from the mother.
The research team also discovered genetic diversity estimated from blow was very similar to estimates from traditional biopsies—with this particular population showing no evidence of inbreeding beyond a shared ancestry or past population bottlenecks.

items.text:
An Arizona community is celebrating a local grandfather who found a missing toddler in the middle of the cold desert night.
Honored by the sheriff’s office as an outstanding citizen, Jay Stewart said he felt what everyone else who was searching felt, saying “she may not be our child, but she could be.”
The story begins at sundown on November 17th, when, playing with her siblings, 2-year-old Vella Campillo wandered off into the desert surrounding the city of Eloy, wearing nothing but a diaper.
Vella’s parents, Joseph Campillo and Deanna Fritz, contacted police shortly after 5 p.m., saying that she was being looked after by another family member but had gone missing. Any parent can relate: one moment a child is there; the next they’re gone.
Pinal County Sheriff’s Office and local volunteers began to scour the area as night closed in and temperatures began to fall. Among them was father and grandfather Jay Stewart.
“The scariest thing for parents is to lose a child,” Stewart told local news. “I can’t imagine what they were going through.” He added that everyone he met was searching for Vella “for the same reason.”
“We loved her and wanted her back—she may not be our child, but she could be.”
Over the next 7 hours, Stewart, along with his fellow volunteers dozens of members from various law enforcement agencies, searched with flashlights amid 50°F temperatures. Drones and a helicopter were involved in the search, but the child’s miniature heat signature rendered the thermal imaging cameras ineffective.
The breakthrough came just after midnight when Stewart was investigating a line of bushes near a ditch where, unbeknownst to him, little Vella lay curled up. He would later call the Sheriff’s office to signal he’d found the girl, who was taken to the hospital after no small amount of convincing, latched as she was onto Stewart with no desire to let go.
She was reunited with her family shortly after with no injuries or hypothermia.

“To find that little scared child, the way she popped out of that bush, I’ll never forget it as long as I live,” Stewart told KZAS.
In a Facebook video from the Sheriff’s Office, Pinal County Sheriff Ross Teeple pronounced Stewart “Pinal County’s hero” and awarded him an outstanding citizen certificate. Teeple also made him an honorary member of the Sheriff’s rescue posse.

items.title: Melinda French Gates Let 12 People Decide How To Give Away $240 Million
items.desc: Melinda French Gates Let 12 People Decide How To Give Away $240 Million In 2024, Melinda French Gates launched the $240 million Global Leaders program, in which she gave $20 million apiece to 12 influential figures to distribute to causes of their choice by the end of 2026. She did this through her philanthropic organization, Pivotal, which works to enact social progress for women and young people
items.text:
Photo: Russell Watkins/Department for International Development via Wikimedia Commons ( CC BY-SA 2.0 )
In 2024, Melinda French Gates launched the $240 million Global Leaders program, in which she gave $20 million apiece to 12 influential figures to distribute to causes of their choice by the end of 2026. She did this through her philanthropic organization, Pivotal , which works to enact social progress for women and young people both in the U.S. and around the world. Now, we’re getting to see the results of her generosity in real time.
French Gates started the program because she recognized the limits of her own perspective when it came to making donations. She wanted the money to reach places where it could make the most impact.
“There are so many great ideas out there that might never cross my path but might cross someone else’s,” she told the Associated Press. “That’s one reason I started the Global Leaders program: to partner with experts whose firsthand knowledge could broaden Pivotal’s perspective and deepen our impact.”
One of the recipients of the money, Dr. Alfiee Breland-Noble, was surprised to be included in the program and has since used the money to fund a wide variety of projects. Breland-Noble, who founded the AAKOMA Project—which stands for African American Knowledge Optimized for Mindfully Healthy Adolescents—to address the mental health needs of young people of color, used the $20 million to establish the MATTIE Fund, short for Mindful Advocacy for Totally Transformative Inclusion and Equity. The fund was also named for and inspired by her mother, Mattie McLeod Breland.
When it came to deciding where the money should go, Breland-Noble even turned to her Instagram followers for suggestions. Among the organizations she supported were BackSpinz Music Academy in North Carolina and Daddy Stroller Social Club, an organization that brings fathers together and raises awareness of paternal postpartum depression.
Another recipient of French Gates’ money was former New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern, who took a slightly different approach with her Matariki Fund for Women. Rather than exclusively donating to existing programs, Ardern wanted to help bring new ones to life. She partnered with the International Rescue Committee to support the creation of Safer Births in Crises, an initiative that works to prevent maternal deaths in areas affected by humanitarian crises. 63 years ago today, the very first episode of Doctor Who was broadcast on the BBC. An Unearthly Child, starring William Hartnell, is set amid a power struggle between warring Stone Age factions who have lost the secret of making fire after the original “companions” Ian and Barbara, find the Doctor’s time-traveling spaceship in a London junkyard. READ about the runup to the debut… (1963)
The show was created to fill a gap between children’s and young adult programming. Canadian producer Sydney Newman, recently made Head of Drama at the BBC, was tasked with creating the show and conceived the idea of the TARDIS, as well as the central character of the Doctor.
The first episode was divided into four separately broadcast parts, but the show’s launch was overshadowed by the assassination of President John F. Kennedy the previous day, resulting in a repeat of the first episode the following week.
Though received with mixed reviews from critics, the “disappointing audience reaction,” averaged between 4 and 6 million viewers—a hit by today’s standards, equivalent to the hyper-successful 30 Rock, and double that of Breaking Bad.
Happy 73rd Birthday to Rick Bayless , perhaps the finest Mexican chef who isn’t Mexican in the United States. Holding a Michelin Star, the inaugural title of Top Chef Master, and 7 James Beard Awards, he has remained a very influential chef in America for many years. Bayless is best known perhaps for a docu-series he made with PBS called Mexico: One Plate at a Time.
In 1978 Bayless hosted the 26-part PBS television series Cooking Mexican, after which the chef dedicated over six years to culinary research in Mexico, culminating in 1987 with the publication of his Authentic Mexican: Regional Cooking from the Heart of Mexico which long-time New York Times restaurant critic Craig Claiborne described as “the greatest contribution to the Mexican table imaginable.”
In 1987, Bayless and his wife Deann opened Frontera Grill in Chicago, specializing in contemporary regional Mexican cuisine, with special emphasis on the varied cuisines of the Oaxaca region. In 1989, Rick and Deann opened Topolobampo, one of Chicago’s first fine-dining Mexican restaurants, and the establishment that was awarded the Michelin Star. (1965)

items.text:
Just in time for the holidays, Good News Network has teamed up with Holstee on a curated collection of gifts that celebrate living well. Shop the collection.
“If you’re looking for the love of your life, stop. They’ll be waiting for you when you start doing the things you love.”
That’s one line from the Holstee Manifesto, a short statement about living well that has been shared across the internet for more than 15 years. Co-founder Michael Radparvar still meets people who say it changed the course of their lives.
“I get chills thinking about it even right now,” Radparvar told GNN. Some tell him it convinced them to travel. Others quit long-held jobs to start businesses of their own. “Almost every line in the manifesto, I would say, has a story that connected with somebody.”
The shirts got buzz on New York fashion blogs. But the brothers, along with their third partner, Fabian, realized the business was never really about T-shirts.
Radparvar remembers the moment clearly. He and Dave were sharing an East Village apartment, with one bedroom stacked with inventory. Dave slid open his bedroom door and announced, “We need a statement that tells the world what we’re about.”
The three hashed it out over long talks in Union Square. Some lines were their own mottos, and others came from family members and people who inspired them. The result sat on their website as plain text for about a year. Then a friend urged them to give it a visual design.
About a week after the designed version went up, it took off on Tumblr, Twitter, and Facebook. “Before we knew it, it just felt like it was everywhere,” Radparvar said.
It caught a moment. Many people in the early 2010s were rethinking their relationship with work and what a happy life meant. “Kind of similar to what it feels like right now, actually,” he said.
Soon the three founders were getting deeply personal messages from strangers. “We’re just guys in our 20s who just put this out there,” Radparvar said. “We don’t know if we’re in a position to tell you whether you should leave your job or change your life or marry this person or not.”
The manifesto even reached author Paulo Coelho, whose account once posted it in a way that suggested he had written it. Holstee’s community corrected the record so fast that, by the time the founders landed from a flight, Coelho had already reached out. It was an honest mistake, Radparvar said, and the team followed up with a playful post: the cover of The Alchemist , credited to Mike, D

items.title: Delia Smith joins opponents of £1.2bn data centre
items.desc: The TV cook and author is worried about the environmental impact of the proposed Keswick facility.
items.text:
Watch: Delia Smith says data centre will be bad for county
Television cook Delia Smith has joined opponents of a £1.2bn data centre, arguing it would threaten a nature reserve.
Campaigners fear the proposed centre at Keswick, on the edge of Norwich, will create noise pollution and have a negative impact on nearby Marston Marsh.
Smith, honorary life president and former majority shareholder of Norwich City FC, said: "I love Norfolk. You can't be involved in a football club for 55 years without being attached to the people and the beauty of Norfolk. I feel very strongly about it."
But developer Norwich Apex said an ecological impact assessment concluded no effect on the reserve was expected.
Delia Smith, pictured with fellow campaigner Jake Humphrey, says she feels very strongly about protecting Norfolk
Data centres are facilities that store and process vast amounts of data and run the software and online services used by millions of people.
This centre, off the A140 Ipswich Road, would need 150 MW of power to run and would feature 72 chiller units on its roof.
According to planning documents, the building would be about 20m (65ft) high.
A planning application for the centre has been lodged with South Norfolk Council.
If approved, construction could begin at the end of 2027 and it would be operational by 2028.
The plans have emerged at the same time as a much bigger proposal for a data centre and solar farm elsewhere in Norfolk, south of King's Lynn, which would require more than five times as much electricity.
What are data centres and are more coming to the East?
The developer has said the Keswick facility would use " air-cooling technology " and not require water for cooling.
But Smith, who lives in Suffolk, said: "We haven't got enough water, and data centres use an awful lot of water.
""It's one of the biggest [data centres] and It doesn't do anything for the Norfolk community. Where is the £1.2bn coming from? And who are the people who are going to presumably make money out of it?
"It's not going to do anything for the local community, it's the opposite. It's going to be bad."
Campaigners have raised concerns about the proposed centre's effect on the nearby Marston Marsh nature reserve
It is hoped the centre will harness wind energy by connecting to the Hornsea 3 substation nearby.
Smith said: "Renewable energy is going into the grid but it doesn't supply everything now.

This year, they will feed 3,600 families in Utah alone. Rob Adams, founder of Thanksgiving Heroes, grew up as the oldest of six children in South Texas. For a stretch […] The post A Childhood Promise Mobilizes ‘Thanksgiving Heroes,’ Serving Thous
items.text:
What began as an 11-year-old boy’s promise to his mother has launched ‘Thanksgiving Heroes,’ a nationwide effort to bring holiday meals to those in need. This year, they will feed 3,600 families in Utah alone.
Rob Adams, founder of Thanksgiving Heroes , grew up as the oldest of six children in South Texas. For a stretch of his childhood, the family lived out of their pickup truck in Porter, an unincorporated area near Houston. They had little clothing and often relied on school lunches as the one guaranteed meal of the day. Adams has said he still remembers being a happy, loved child, but the hardship was real.
One Christmas, a neighboring family—the Christiansons—drove the Adams family about 12 miles to their home in Kingwood. The house was picture-perfect, complete with a Christmas tree. The Christiansons were leaving for the holidays and invited the Adams family to stay while they were gone.
They left the refrigerator fully stocked with turkey, pumpkin pie, and other food, with presents for the children under the tree. The gesture of unconditional kindness left a lasting mark. At 11, Adams told his mother that one day, when he was “rich,” which at the time simply meant not sleeping in their car, he would pay it forward. “I feel like I owe this to another family because someone was so kind to me,” Adams said.
Years later, as his mother faced a brain-cancer diagnosis, she reminded him of that childhood vow and urged him to follow through. That push led Adams to launch Thanksgiving Heroes.
Adams set a modest goal the first year: feed 10 families. Instead, Thanksgiving Heroes provided meals to about 755 families. This year, the group aims to reach 3,600 families across Utah , but the fulfillment of Adams’ promise extends beyond state lines.
Thanksgiving Heroes has grown into a national network of local affiliates that together have served more than 29,000 families. While the Utah chapter remains the largest—having provided meals to nearly 20,000 families since 2015—the model has spread through independent affiliates that receive support from the parent foundation.
Established chapters now operate in Cleveland, Ohio (more than 6,600 families since 2020) and Las Vegas (hundreds of families since 2021), while newer affiliates have launched in Phoenix, Orange County, California, Stark County, Ohio, and New Haven, Connecticut. Although visitors can’t meet the newest arrivals in person just yet, they can watch the family bond, play, and nap together through the zoo’s live Cheetah Cub Cam.
items.text:
Cheetah cubs inside the den of Zura, a 5-year-old cheetah. Her five cubs were born Oct. 5, 2026, at the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute (SCBI) in Front Royal, VA. The cubs do not have names yet. Their gender is currently unknown. They are currently on the Cheetah Cub Cam hosted on the Zoo’s website.
Born October 5, 2026, at the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute in Front Royal, Va., five cubs are growing up under the watchful eye of their mother, Zura. Although visitors can’t meet the newest arrivals in person just yet, they can watch the family bond, play, and nap together through the zoo’s live Cheetah Cub Cam .
Zura is a first-time mother at 5 years old, and her cubs are reported to be healthy, strong, and active. For now, animal care staff are keeping their distance to give the family time to bond, while monitoring their progress through the livestream. The first few weeks are especially important for young cheetahs as they develop a close relationship with their mother, who provides their food, warmth, and protection.
The new litter is also important for the Smithsonian’s conservation program. Zura’s five cubs represent the 21st litter born at the facility since 2007. This litter marks the fourth generation of the same cheetah family now living at the conservation institute. Zura was born there in 2021, her mother Rosalie arrived in 2015, and her grandmother Sanurra also lives at the facility.
Cheetahs are classified as vulnerable, with fewer than 7,000 estimated to remain in the wild due to habitat loss, declining prey populations, climate change, poaching, and conflict with humans. Breeding cheetahs in human care is not an easy task, either. Females have relatively short and unpredictable periods of fertility, and successful pairings can be difficult to achieve. Cheetahs also have limited genetic diversity because their ancestors experienced a severe population decline thousands of years ago.
The Smithsonian currently cares for approximately 30 cheetahs at its Front Royal conservation campus, where researchers and animal care specialists work to improve the species’ long-term prospects. They expect the cubs to remain visible on the livestream for approximately six to seven months, although they may occasionally disappear from view as Zura moves them around their habitat.

items.title: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
items.desc: The report says there are signs of possible contamination across almost all of Gaza as a result of Israel's actions.
items.text:
The UN estimates that Israeli forces dropped more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives on Gaza in almost two years (file photo)
Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the charity Oxfam says , external .
Heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and dioxins and biological contaminants are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.
Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, said the impact on Gaza "will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival".
In response, the Israeli embassy in the UK said the report "falls short of professional standards".
Behar also accused Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza".
Israel has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. It maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.
The report says 99% of Gaza shows indicators of potential environmental contamination
Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.
The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".
Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.

items.title: More Than 50 Dancers Will Celebrate Our Connection to the Ocean During Miami Art Week
items.desc: More Than 50 Dancers Will Celebrate Our Connection to the Ocean During Miami Art Week As part of Miami Art Week, more than 50 dancers and members of the public will come together on Miami Beach to celebrate our deep and lasting relationship with the sea. The Ocean Odyssey is a new, site-specific performance by Indian artist Subodh Kerkar, presented in partnership with the Andaz Miami Beach Resort
items.text:
As part of Miami Art Week, more than 50 dancers and members of the public will come together on Miami Beach to celebrate our deep and lasting relationship with the sea. The Ocean Odyssey is a new, site-specific performance by Indian artist Subodh Kerkar , presented in partnership with the Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa , the Miami City Ballet , and its artistic director, Gonzalo García.
Kerkar describes the ocean as “a symbol of celebration of one humanity,” adding, “I celebrate the inseparability of human life and the ocean.” The artist is inviting up to 60 members of the public to join professional dancers in the performance. Together, they’ll move across the beach in a carefully choreographed sequence, creating lines and shapes—like straight lines, wavy lines, and circle formations—that are particularly striking when viewed from above. As Kerkar explains , “No dance experience needed: it begins as a simple walk, and from above, it becomes something extraordinary.”
The Ocean Odyssey will take place on Dec. 4, between 4-5 p.m., in front of Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa. It’s organized by REEFLINE , a non-profit and pioneering underwater public sculpture park at Miami Beach. REEFLINE is creating a new kind of underwater reef, bringing together art, science, and technology to support marine restoration, encourage biodiversity, and help ocean ecosystems thrive.
Check out some photos from one of Kerkar’s previous performances below to get a glimpse of what to expect during Miami Art Week.

items.title: Good News in History, November 24
items.desc: 167 years ago today, the British naturalist and geologist Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species explaining his theory of evolution. The first edition—which has been voted by publishers and librarians as the most influential academic book ever written—introduced the scientific theory that populations evolve over the course of generations through a process of […] The post Good News in Hi
items.text:
167 years ago today, the British naturalist and geologist Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species explaining his theory of evolution. The first edition—which has been voted by publishers and librarians as the most influential academic book ever written—introduced the scientific theory that populations evolve over the course of generations through a process of natural selection. It presented a body of evidence that the diversity of life arose by common descent through a tree-like branching pattern of evolution. WATCH an animation about how little finches were crucial to his discovery, and how pepper moths evolved due to pollution… (1859)
Darwin included evidence that he had gathered on expeditions to South America in the 1830s and his subsequent findings from research and experimentation, and showed how natural selection is a scientifically testable mechanism. Within two decades widespread scientific agreement solidified that evolution had occurred, and by the mid-20th century Darwin’s concept of evolutionary adaptation through natural selection became central to modern evolutionary theory—and the unifying concept of the life sciences.
Modern evolutionary theory continues to develop, but his writings still explain the diversity of living organisms and their adaptation to the environment; make sense of the geological record; and hold up under modern genome analysis.
Because of church teachings at the time, his theory was much maligned, but clergymen later came to accept natural selection, explaining it as an instrument of God’s design. The Vatican stated its official position in 1950, which held that evolution was consistent with Catholic teachings. Darwin, himself, believed at the outset that God had been creating life through the laws of nature.

items.title: Record 5,200 heat-linked deaths estimated in England this year
items.desc: The UK Health Security Agency says this year's number of deaths is twice that of the previous record year.
items.text:
An estimated 5,258 deaths in England were associated with this summer's hot weather
More than 5,000 people suffered heat-associated deaths in England this summer, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has estimated - the highest number since records began in 2016.
The UK experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, and the estimated 5,258 heat-linked deaths were twice the previous high of 2,985 in 2022.
The most deadly period of the year for heat-related deaths was between 21 and 28 June, when there were an estimated 2,401 heat-associated deaths. Temperatures peaked at 38C in that period.
Climate change is expected to increase the length, frequency and intensity of extreme heat, the UKHSA has warned.
The UKHSA said summer 2026 was "exceptional", and that it recorded the highest annual number of heat episodes, which it defines as days when the average Central England Temperature (CET) is at least 20C.
There were seven heat episodes between May and August, adding up to a total of 41 days.
The UK experienced widespread heatwaves as 2026 became the hottest summer on record, according to provisional data from the Met Office.
A heatwave in May smashed the temperature record for that month by more than 2C, with a high of 35.1C recorded at Kew Gardens.
A month later, June's heatwave set another monthly temperature record - 38.0C in Lingwood, Norfolk. The previous high was 35.6C set in 1957 and equalled during the infamous 1976 heatwave.
Both were caused by heat domes - stalled areas of high pressure that trap hot air over the region.
Another heatwave in mid-August saw temperatures climb as high as 38.2C at Hartpury College in Gloucestershire, making it the hottest day of the year.
The UK's hottest day on record was 19 July 2022, when temperatures hit 40.3C in Coningsby, Lincolnshire.
A lack of rainfall this year also saw droughts declared in all of Wales and more than two-thirds of England, while wildfires caused devastation in some parts of the country.
UKHSA said the findings "underline the need for longer-term adaptation" to a warming climate, and that adapting homes, neighbourhoods and health and care settings would be "increasingly important".
Dr Ross Thompson, principal environmental health scientist at UKHSA, said this summer's hot weather had a substantial impact on public health, "particularly during the early heat episodes in May and June".

items.title: Charity Swaps Tuition Fees for Coconuts So Every Islander Can Afford School
items.desc: The coconut palm is often called the Tree of 1,000 Uses, though ‘school tuition voucher’ is not typically one of those 1,000. Yet the Faith Christian Academy in Micronesia is, in fact, accepting coconuts in lieu of tuition costs—to help ease the financial burden on families while making use of the ubiquitous fruits that pile […] The post Charity Swaps Tuition Fees for Coconuts So Every Islander Ca
items.text:
The coconut palm is often called the Tree of 1,000 Uses, though ‘school tuition voucher’ is not typically one of those 1,000.
Yet the Faith Christian Academy in Micronesia is, in fact, accepting coconuts in lieu of tuition costs—to help ease the financial burden on families while making use of the ubiquitous fruits that pile up all around.
The Academy’s new tuition plan actually clears 2 hurdles in 1 leap. Students can easily afford tuition while sparing themselves the dangers and toil of fishing to make money. On the other, the coconuts are used by the Academy to rebuild Yap Island’s once-flourishing coconut oil industry.
“Yap is beautiful, but cash is hard to come by,” says Paul Zimmer, founder and CEO of 3 different organizations working on Yap Island, including the Academy. “Almost every family lives off the land and sea. 95% of households grow crops, 88% fish, and 78% grow coconuts, nearly all for their own table.”
“We asked a simple question: what if the thing Yap has in abundance could help pay for the thing families want most for their kids?”
Zimmer would go on to tell GNN that only one-third of all islanders had cash-paying work, most of which was through the government. The notion of a local economy is almost a dream. Everything needed that can’t be grown is imported, and virtually nothing is exported. That wasn’t always the case, however.
According to Zimmer, this island state within the Federated States of Micronesia used to be a large exporter of virgin coconut oil, but slowing exports through the ’90s stopped entirely by the mid-2000s “because prices were low, shipping was poor, and the palms were aging.”
Though the market was gone, the coconuts kept on growing. At the same time, a decade of balancing the books at Faith Christian Academy (FCA) demonstrated that students would often have to work themselves to the bone to afford the tuition costs.
At times, this would involve dangerous nighttime fishing, while at other times it meant double shifts at work for low-wage earners: like the father of Shayalynn, whose family is from the outer island of Ifaluk, but who has attended FCA since 2017.
“I felt relieved and happy about it because my dad didn’t have to work a lot for my tuition,” she said, remembering when she first heard about the coconuts, “The first year that I started in FCA in 2017, he had to work double shifts just to be able to pay for my tuition, the food on the table, and the clothes that I had to wear to school.”

items.title: 89 Memes That Are So Relatable You Might Think You Never Had An Original Experience
items.desc: Sometimes you don't have to look very far to find comedy. Life serves up plenty of its own, like a mannequin giving off serious "I'll wait until you're all quiet" teacher energy, or a minivan carrying enough watermelons to star in a math word problem. Moments like these are easy to miss, but they're impossible to forget once someone adds the perfect bit of commentary. Here are some of the funniest
items.text:
One meme on this list shows a stop sign peeking out from a tangle of leaves. On its own, it's a pretty mundane sight. Relatable? Sure, especially if you live somewhere where trimming the trees isn't exactly top priority. But it only takes one simple line of text to take it to the next level: "When your friend is about to do something kinda stupid but you wanna see what happens." Suddenly, you've never related more to a street sign (even if you’d never admit it).
That leafy meme reminded me of a project from my fine art printmaking days, when we were given a brief exploring the relationship between image and text. The idea was simple enough: put words and images side by side, and see what happens to the meaning of each. Turns out, a few words can completely change what you think you're looking at.
Of course, artists have been playing with that tension for centuries. One particularly influential example is René Magritte's 1929 painting of a pipe, with the words "Ceci n'est pas une pipe" ("This is not a pipe") written underneath. At first, the words seem to contradict what's right in front of you. Then it clicks: it really isn't a pipe; it's just a picture of one.
Those few words make you stop and think about what you're actually looking at. In fact, as art historian Julien Delagrange explains , Magritte helped establish the idea that text isn't just a way of communicating, but "a structural element in the production of meaning itself." But the idea of reusing images with new words goes back way further than Magritte.
Never miss a story that brings joy to the world. Add us on Google
In 17th-century England, for example, woodcut illustrations were expensive to make, so printers reused the same blocks to illustrate all kinds of different ballads. Researcher Katie Sisneros calls these reused woodcuts "proto-memes." One stock figure, nicknamed the "how-de-do man," turned up in more than 100 surviving ballads. Most of the time he was an okay-enough guy. In one, he was recast as a cruel husband.
Sisneros compares him to a much more recent image: the " distracted boyfriend " stock photo. It started life as a fairly forgettable picture of a man turning to look at another woman while his girlfriend stares at him in disbelief. Then the internet got hold of it, adding endless new labels to turn it into a commentary on everything from—well, you've seen them.
Tell us. It helps us improve the new Bored Panda.

items.desc: A major success in population-scale control of mosquito-borne viruses comes now from Brazil, where schoolchildren are enjoying a 68% lower risk of such diseases. The trial tested the largely-proven method of releasing mosquitoes infected with Wolbachia bacteria, which inhibits the insect’s ability to spread viruses like dengue, Zika, and chikungunya. Trialed over 4 years in […] The post Major Succ
items.text:
A major success in population-scale control of mosquito-borne viruses comes now from Brazil, where schoolchildren are enjoying a 68% lower risk of such diseases.
The trial tested the largely-proven method of releasing mosquitoes infected with Wolbachia bacteria, which inhibits the insect’s ability to spread viruses like dengue, Zika, and chikungunya.
Trialed over 4 years in Belo Horizonte, the success overlapped with the largest outbreak of dengue fever ever recorded in Brazil, demonstrating the urgent need for greater mosquito control in the tropics.
“The intervention substantially reduced dengue infections during Brazil’s largest recorded outbreak, demonstrating its potential to protect communities even under conditions of intense transmission,” states Derek Cummings, PhD, co-principal investigator of the trial and Bloomberg Distinguished Professor at Johns Hopkins University, one of the institutions that participated.
Called the EVITA dengue trial, the international team set out to test a locally-adapted version of the wMel strain of Wolbachia for use in inhibiting viral transmission from Aedes aegypti mosquitoes.
wMel is the most commonly-used strain of Wolbachia, with the ‘Mel’ referring to the fruit fly species from which Wolbachia was first isolated. wMel-infected mosquitoes pass the bacteria to their offspring, thereby inhibiting disease transmission on a generational scale.
EVITA included 58 school-defined geographic clusters in Belo Horizonte, with 29 clusters assigned to receive releases of wMel mosquitoes in addition to standard vector-control measures, and 29 clusters assigned to standard vector control alone, such as insecticidal sprays and mosquito source reduction.
The randomized-controlled trial released Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes from January 2021 through May 2022. It involved 5,757 school children, ages 6 to 11. The results were presented on Saturday at the American Society of Tropical Medicine & Hygiene annual meeting in National Harbor, Maryland.

The Moon’s brightest period will come at 9:40 a.m. US Eastern Time on Tuesday, but dark periods either side of this moment will still make for great viewing, with the difference in illumination being […] The post First of 3 Consecutive Supermoons to Begin Tonight – Look to the Eas
items.text:
The next 3 consecutive full moons will weigh in as supermoons—and the first one is set to dazzle tonight and tomorrow.
The Moon’s brightest period will come at 9:40 a.m. US Eastern Time on Tuesday, but dark periods either side of this moment will still make for great viewing, with the difference in illumination being almost imperceptible.
Hanging in the middle of the firmament, supermoons don’t look much bigger than normal full moons. Rather, it’s when they’re close to the horizon that they take on their super appearance.
That’s down to an optical illusion created by trees and houses that make the Moon appear bigger by comparison. Take the opportunity to experience the illusion by dressing warmly and stepping out into an open area in the early twilight tonight and tomorrow night to catch moonrise in the eastern sky.
This month’s moon is being called the Beaver Moon , as it’s the time when beavers would head to their dens for hibernation. Native tribes, like the Dakota and Lakota, have their own terms for the November moon—the Deer Rutting Moon, in this case.
The Cree called it the Frost Moon, while the Tlingit called it the Digging, or Scratching Moon, a reference to animals pawing the hard earth looking for sustenance.
A moon becomes a supermoon when it reaches ‘perigee’ or the closest point to Earth in its orbit (this is as opposed to apogee, the farthest point in orbit from Earth, which produces a ‘micromoon’).
The Beaver Moon will begin a series of 3 consecutive supermoons, with another appearing in December and a third in January—perfect reasons to brave the cold and get out in nature, or to walk off those hearty winter dinners.
December’s Cold Moon will be the biggest of the 3, with its fullest phase corresponding to an even closer point of perigee in its orbit around our planet, while January’s Wolf Moon will also be a supermoon.

items.title: China's Shenzhou-24 carries Pakistan's first astronaut into space
items.desc: Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a former fighter pilot, is the first foreigner to join a Chinese crewed space mission.
items.text:
Historic space mission lifts off with first Pakistani astronaut aboard Chinese rocket
China launched its Shenzhou-24 space mission on Wednesday carrying three astronauts to its Tiangong space station, including Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to join a Chinese crewed space mission.
Beijing said it hopes the flight will strengthen ties with Islamabad, as the two countries mark 75 years of co-operation in space.
Speaking to reporters at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, Ali said he was "carrying the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis".
The mission, which also comprises of commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi, took off at 08:18 (00:18 GMT) from the Gobi desert. Minutes later, it was declared a "complete success".
While in space, the Shenzhou-24 crew will carry out experiments and test technology in fields like aerospace medicine, combustion and study the effects of space on living organisms.
The mission comprises of payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, flight engineer Wu Yi and commander Tang Hongbo
They will also study how the space environment affects aging, with the hope of developing new ways to prevent and treat age-related vascular diseases.
Ali will conduct studies on photosynthesis in bacteria and the effects of radiation and microgravity - a very weak gravity in space - on seeds.
The former fighter pilot will return to Earth after a short stay, with two other Chinese crew members who have been at the space station since May.
Tang and Wu will spend six months at Tiangong space station along with Zhu Yangzhu, a member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, which lifted off in May this year. Zhu has been studying how the human body adapts to long periods in space.
The Shenzhou-24 is also a diplomatic moment for Beijing.
China has poured billions of dollars into its space programme and its prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.
It is now keen to show the world that the station has the potential to become an international research platform rather than an exclusive Chinese facility.
Hundreds of people gathered at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center before dawn waving Chinese and Pakistani flags.

items.text:
A new thumb implant is transforming hand function for people with advanced arthritis.
Traditionally, doctors remove the trapezium, a small bone at the thumb’s base
To overcome “bone-on-bone contact” the new treatment that uses a “ball-and-socket” designed as an insert for repairing the trapezium.
In trials, patients who received the thumb implants gained a range of motion—and it stayed stronger over the long term.
Thumb arthritis (carpometacarpal osteoarthritis) is a debilitating condition that effects millions of Americans and can dramatically impact hand use and daily quality of life.
Performed more than 130,000 times in Europe since gaining approval there, its use is now spreading across the United States after receiving FDA approval last year.
The Swiss-designed CMC Touch 1 prosthesis, developed and manufactured by KeriMedical, does not require any anatomy changes. Surgeons use the same approach they are already familiar with—like a mini hip replacement for the thumb.
“The mechanics of it are a ball and socket joint to replace the saddle joint that is your thumb,” said orthopedic surgeon Dr. Stephen Berling, who was trained in the procedure in Ohio.
Traditional thumb reconstruction is used when bone-on-bone arthritis occurs where the thumb meets the wrist. The procedure involves removing the trapezium bone and then resuspending the thumb, but there are big downsides.
The thumb may take time to function properly without the bone, requiring a lengthy recovery of six to nine months, with patients in a splint or cast for 6 weeks.
On the other hand, recent patients who’ve receive the TOUCH prosthesis, which helps restore pinch and grip strength, are leaving the operating room with just an ACE bandage.
With this new implant, the bone is not removed, which provides immediate stability and helps accelerate recovery. The outpatient surgery takes about 45 minutes, allows patients to go home the same day. (Stitches stay in for two weeks, and once they are removed, patients can shower and get their hand wet.)

items.text:
A one-time infusion of CRISPR gene editing therapy slashed dangerous cholesterol by 52%, with the patients still experiencing the benefit 12 months after initial treatment, and without side effects.
The Cleveland Clinic in Ohio reported that their Phase 1 human trial showed a one-time infusion of a gene-editing therapy using CRISPR-Cas9 was effective and safe in reducing “bad” LDL cholesterol and triglycerides by nearly half in patients throughout a one-year follow-up, after their disorder had previously been resistant to medication.
The trial, which included 15 patients, aimed to see if the reductions in LDL cholesterol and triglycerides previously reported after two months would persist for 12 months. After 12 months, patients who were treated with the highest dose saw a 52.5% lowering from baseline in LDL cholesterol, and a 47.8% reduction in triglycerides. There were no serious adverse events related to the therapy during the one-year follow-up.
The study, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in August, was funded by CRISPR Therapeutics AG in Switzerland.
“The durability of the lipid-lowering effect was impressive,” said Cleveland Clinic cardiologist Dr. Luke Laffin, the first author of the study.
“It is encouraging that there were no serious safety events related to CTX310 in the trial and in the year following treatment. We look forward to continuing to investigate this therapy in a larger number of patients.”
CRISPR-Cas9 is a gene-editing technology that can be used to modify or correct specific regions of a person’s DNA to treat serious diseases.
This trial tested CTX310, an experimental CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing treatment that is delivered as a one-time infusion. CTX310 carries the CRISPR editing mechanism into the liver, where it switches off a gene called ANGPTL3. Turning off this gene can lower LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, which are both linked to heart disease.

During the trial, CTX310 was administered at doses from 0.1 to 0.8 mg/kg during the single infusion, after pre-treatment with corticosteroids and antihistamines. Participants were monitored for safety of the treatment, and the effects of this gene therapy on ANGPTL3, LDL cholesterol and triglyceride levels. CTX310 reduced both LDL cholesterol and triglycerides by approximately 50% on average at the highest dose 12 months after the treatment.

items.text:
A Canadian man is writing a coda into the lives of scrapped musical instruments by using them to offer a free lunch to his feathered neighbors.
A nibble of corn or seed comes with no strings attached at the Frets and Feathers Cafe, run by retired teacher Rob Burke from Prince Edward Island.
The former math teacher saw someone from Europe make an old guitar into a birdfeeder on social media and figured he could do one better: a three-course orchestra.
Asking for donations of broken instruments for an art project on Facebook, Burke was delighted to receive 6 guitars, an old violin, and pieces of a drum set.
He got to work attaching driftwood perches and metal feeding dishes into the hollow-body guitars.
CBC reported that his choice of a glue gun was just fine at first, but once the heavier blue jays began visiting, he had to reattach the perches and dishes more firmly.
His Facebook wall features an array of common birds, which Burke says he has taken a greater interest in since retiring. Videos are often paired with music, and make for great viewing.
He has since seen a woodpecker, corvids, and chickadees, and expects to see further species as the seasons change.
For any other PE Islanders, Burke welcomes further instrument donations to expand the Peck and Play Orchestra. One can contact him over Facebook.

items.text:
In 1967, 33 Massachusetts schoolchildren were given a project: write a letter to a Navy corpsman they had never met who was wounded in Vietnam.
None of them had any idea of the impact their letters had on the veteran, until his son, almost 60 years later, began searching them out.
“I just needed to get back to them and be like, ‘Hey, I know it seems really silly, you’re talking about your pet lizard and you’re saying God bless you, but it made a difference,'” Dave Jacobson tells GNN.
Dave’s father was HM3 Russell Jacobson, who suffered 12 gunshot wounds and shrapnel from a grenade blast. He had been brought home to an understaffed Chelsea Naval Hospital and put in a full-body cast.
Outside, protestors against the Vietnam war heaped abuse on returning servicemen, and for Russell, who Dave described as entering the war as a “pacifist” with the aim of “healing people,” there was a sense of shame, which together with his injuries, began to seep into his very soul.
“He was non-verbal for many weeks and he was refusing food and water, and was down to about 80 pounds. He had lost a dozen of his friends in a couple of hours,” Dave, who wouldn’t be born for another 10 years, explained.
“My mom was a nurse and one of her co-workers was named Kitty. She was always kind of like grasping at straws, like ‘How can we to get this guy back on his feet?'”
“Her sister was a nun at a Catholic school in Gloucester, and she made all the kids write these letters of support.”
It wasn’t as if his father hadn’t been receiving letters: he had, from friends and colleagues, all of whom wrote “kind of what they think they should say.” But it was when Corpsman Russell opened the envelope of 33 letters from St. Ann School and began to leaf through them that, as Kitty said, he began to get back onto his feet.
Slowly, Russell and his wife began to read through the letters, each sealed with a small yearbook-style photo of the author. A boy named Peter talks about his pet lizard, two others talk about how crazy it was that Peter brought his lizard to school. Another asks, as if on the phone, whether Russell knew what was going on with the Montreal Expos’ season.
“You could just tell a lot of these kids knew they weren’t going to get a call back but, they’re writing these sweet things from the bottom of their heart, like ‘Hey I’m gonna be praying for you every night.’ ‘Remember that I need you to get home safely and need you to come visit me when you’re better.'”

items.text:
American conservationists have secured protections for a truly unique-in-the-world ecosystem along the state’s Bering Sea coastline.
Home to the largest concentrations of Pacific walrus found anywhere in North America, the barrier islands off the coast of the tiny northern village of Point Lay provide a critical refuge for these marine megafauna.
Now ensconced within a 47,000-acre protected area (74 square miles) held by the Interior Alaska Land Trust, the islands have been spared from industrial development and other disturbances, as has “one of the largest, undiminished coastal lagoon systems in the world,” which was protected in tandem.
Part of the coalition that for 10 years has worked towards securing protections for the Point Lay barrier islands and the Kasegaluk Lagoon, The Conservation Fund explains that the islands hadn’t historically been a walrus mecca until 2007, when the animals changed their seasonal migration behavior in mass.
Every year, a quarter million Pacific walrus would migrate north through the Bering Strait, with the males remaining out at sea and the females with their calves moving towards the shallow, nutrient-rich waters of the Chukchi Sea between Alaska and Russia.
Historically, these animals relied on Arctic sea ice for resting spots, but by 2007 the ice had become inconsistent. One year, an estimated 200,000 walrus hauled themselves up onto the barrier islands of Point Lay, and they’ve returned every year ever since.
That includes every single female and juvenile Pacific walrus on Earth—all stuffed onto beaches that will now forever be theirs thanks to The Conservation Fund and its partners among the Alaska tribal nations and the Interior Alaska Land Trust.
The new conservation easement was bought by the Fund from an Alaska Native Corporation the Cully Corp. It will be held by the Trust, which will increase monitoring and stewardship to actively minimize disturbance to walrus and other animals as commercial and tourist activity in the Alaskan Arctic continues to expand. Conservation Fund noted that encroachment from humans had already caused undesirable stampede events among the resting animals.
